name: Money Mindset Test
tagline: Discover your money personality and the habits that suit it.
intro: This test reveals your money mindset: the attitudes and habits that shape how you earn, spend, save and think about money. It compares five money personalities (the Saver, the Spender, the Avoider, the Status Seeker and the Security Seeker) and shows which one fits you best. Answer honestly based on how you usually behave. It takes about five minutes and gives you concrete money habits that match your style.
seoTitle: Money Mindset Test: Discover your money personality
seoDescription: Saver, spender or avoider? Take this free 5-minute money mindset test, discover your money personality and get practical habits for your finances.

saver.name: The Saver
saver.short: Enjoys keeping money, tracking spending and finding good deals.
saver.low: Saving is not a strong driver for you. You may spend fairly freely and see budgets as restrictive. This can make life feel spontaneous, but it can also leave you without a buffer when unexpected costs appear. Try automating savings: set up a small transfer to a separate account on payday, so saving happens before you can spend. Even a modest amount each month builds a cushion over time without requiring constant willpower.
saver.mid: You save when it makes sense but also allow yourself to enjoy your money. This balanced approach is healthy for most people. To make it even stronger, give your savings a clear purpose, such as a holiday, an emergency fund or a future goal. Named goals are easier to stick to. A simple rule like saving a fixed percentage of every income and spending the rest freely keeps both sides in balance.
saver.high: Your answers suggest the Saver is a strong part of your money personality. You like seeing your savings grow, compare prices and feel good about spending less. This discipline is a real strength for long-term security. The risk is that saving becomes so important that you deny yourself things that matter or feel guilty about any spending. Try setting a monthly 'guilt-free' budget for enjoyment. If worry about spending causes ongoing stress, a qualified financial counsellor or other professional can help.

spender.name: The Spender
spender.short: Enjoys using money for pleasure, treats, experiences and generosity.
spender.low: Spending does not hold much excitement for you. You are unlikely to buy on impulse and probably think carefully before purchases. This protects your finances well. Just make sure you also allow yourself to enjoy your money now and then: experiences, gifts and small treats can add real value to life. Consider planning one deliberate treat a month that you look forward to and enjoy without second-guessing.
spender.mid: You enjoy spending but usually keep it within limits. Treats and experiences matter to you, yet you also keep an eye on the bigger picture. To stay in balance, use a simple waiting rule: for non-essential purchases above a certain amount, wait 48 hours before buying. If you still want it, go ahead. Also check your bank statement monthly to see whether your spending matches what you truly value.
spender.high: Your answers suggest the Spender is a strong part of your money personality. You enjoy shopping, treats and experiences, and spending may lift your mood. Generosity and enjoying life are real strengths, but impulse buys can leave you short before the month ends. Try a separate 'fun money' account with a fixed monthly amount, and unsubscribe from shop newsletters. If spending feels hard to control, leads to debt or affects your wellbeing, a qualified financial counsellor or other professional can help.

avoider.name: The Avoider
avoider.short: Tends to put off, ignore or feel stressed by money matters.
avoider.low: You seem to face money matters fairly directly. You check your accounts, deal with bills and feel reasonably confident handling finances. This awareness is a strong foundation for good decisions. Keep it up with a short monthly money check-in where you review your balance, upcoming bills and goals. You might also deepen your knowledge, for example by learning more about pensions or investing, to make your confidence even more useful.
avoider.mid: You handle money matters, but sometimes only when you have to. Certain topics, such as retirement or paperwork, may feel uncomfortable and get postponed. Try scheduling a fixed 20-minute 'money date' each week to open post, pay bills and check your balance. Making it routine removes the need for motivation. Start with the task you have been avoiding longest, as it often brings the biggest sense of relief.
avoider.high: Your answers suggest the Avoider is a strong part of your money personality. Money may feel stressful or confusing, so you put off checking accounts, opening bills or making decisions. This is very common, but avoidance usually makes problems grow. Start small: check your balance once a day for a week, set up automatic bill payments and list your subscriptions. Ask a trusted person to help. If money worries weigh heavily on your wellbeing, a qualified debt adviser, financial counsellor or other professional can help.

status_seeker.name: The Status Seeker
status_seeker.short: Sees money as a way to show success and gain recognition.
status_seeker.low: Status does not seem to drive your money choices. You care little about brands or what others think of your possessions, and you are comfortable living modestly. This frees you from costly comparisons. Keep spending in line with your own values. Just make sure you do not underinvest in things that genuinely help you, such as quality tools or clothing for your work, simply to avoid looking flashy.
status_seeker.mid: You care somewhat about how your lifestyle looks to others, but it does not dominate your choices. A nice brand or a shared holiday photo can feel good, and that is normal. To keep it in check, ask before bigger purchases: would I still want this if nobody else saw it? Muting accounts on social media that make you feel behind can also reduce the pressure to keep up.
status_seeker.high: Your answers suggest the Status Seeker is a strong part of your money personality. Money and possessions may feel linked to success, confidence and how others see you. Ambition can be motivating, but keeping up appearances can be expensive and leave you feeling never quite enough. Try a 30-day pause on status purchases and notice how you feel. Define success in your own terms, too. If comparison or spending pressure affects your wellbeing, a qualified financial counsellor or other professional can help.

security_seeker.name: The Security Seeker
security_seeker.short: Values stability, safety nets and protection against financial risk.
security_seeker.low: Financial security is not a top concern for you. You are comfortable with risk and uncertainty, which can open doors to exciting opportunities. The downside is that you may lack a safety net when things go wrong. Build a basic emergency fund of at least one month of essential costs before taking big risks, and check whether you have the most important insurance in place. That base lets you take chances more safely.
security_seeker.mid: You value stability, but you are also open to some risk. This balance helps you protect yourself while still growing. To strengthen it, aim for an emergency fund covering three to six months of essential costs and review your insurance once a year. For investments, consider a simple mix that matches your timeline, so you can stay calm during ups and downs without avoiding growth altogether.
security_seeker.high: Your answers suggest the Security Seeker is a strong part of your money personality. Safety nets, stable income and avoiding risk matter a lot to you. This makes you prepared and resilient. The risk is that worry about the future crowds out enjoying the present, or that excessive caution limits growth. Once your emergency fund is in place, consider learning about low-cost, diversified investing. If financial worries feel constant or affect your sleep or mood, a qualified financial counsellor or other professional can help.

summary: Everyone has a mix of money attitudes. Below you see how strongly each of five money personalities shows up in your answers, from 0 to 100 %. Your highest score is your main money type, but the other scores matter too. No type is good or bad; each has strengths and blind spots. This report is not financial advice.
